chapter: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
title: Why he wrote long, complex pieces from age 19
summary: Jazz players limited themselves to one tempo and meter; he loved Stravinsky, Debussy, Ravel, Strauss.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well, that's all right. I think you've been very eloquent. I'm very pleased with what we have on tape. Surprised the hell out of me a couple of times, though, Charles. What -- I don't know if we touched on this before, but why did you feel such a need to write, even when you were 19, and the things you were writing were very complex and long and with many movements and tempo changes. Why did you feel the need to express yourself that way, as opposed to doing someting that would be easier to get played, or --

I just always felt that jazz guys hadn't progressed, that they were limiting themselves by playing in one tempo. And also, one meter. Because I listened to a different kind of music. I was in love with Stravinsky and Debussy, a little bit with Ravel. What's the guy that wrote Death and Transfigurations?
Richard Strauss. I heard very little Beethoven and Bartok then, other than school, but when I heard it, I didn't like it, until I grew up and heard string quartets of --
